Key: straw, clear to somewhat hazy, large dense white head, poor retention; pilsner malt + wheat malt (often at least half); symbiotic co-fermentation of top-fermenting yeast and LAB (Lacto) gives sharpness; blending of ages and cool aging; decoction mash with mash hopping traditional; German scientists consider Brett essential for fruity-floral profile but Brett character restrained (not funky); aged examples may show cider/honey/hay notes; German Schankbier 7-8 P. Fruited/spiced versions go to 29A/30A/29B.
Comparison: vs Lambic, clean lactic sourness with restrained/sub-threshold Brett, lower alcohol; vs Straight Sour and Catharina Sour, lower gravity and may contain Brett.
Examples: Bayerischer Bahnhof Berliner Style Weisse, Berliner Berg Berliner Weisse, Brauerei Meierei Weisse, Lemke Berlin Budike Weisse, Schell's Schelltheiss, Urban Chestnut Ku'damm.

styles.name: Flanders Red Ale
text: Aroma: complex fruity-sour with supporting malt; high fruit (black cherry, orange, plum, red currant, fruit leather); low to med-low vanilla/chocolate/peppery phenol; moderate to high sour; dominant vinegar inappropriate (low-mod acetic OK if balanced); no hop aroma.

Flavor: moderate to mod-high soft toasty-rich malt; intense fruit; complex moderate-high sourness accentuated by esters (not simple lactic); vinegar not dominant (low-mod acetic OK); as sour rises, malt fades; low-med-low vanilla/chocolate/pepper optional; no hop flavor; restrained bitterness, malt-leaning; acids and tannins give structure; sweetness varies (blended/sweetened versions).
Mouthfeel: medium body, tannin-enhanced; low to medium carbonation; low-med astringency, prickly acidity; light and crisp though somewhat sweet finish not uncommon.

Key: deep red/burgundy-brown, wine-like (not literally); aged up to 2 years in large oak foeders; blend of young and old beer, variable sweetening; Vienna/Munich malts, caramel malts, maize, low-alpha continental hops; Sacch + Lacto + Brett; vinegar has 6x total acidity of this style. Fruited versions to 29A. Rodenbach tradition.
Comparison: less malt-rich than Oud Bruin, often more fruity-tart and acetic.
Examples: Cuvee des Jacobins Rouge, Duchesse de Bourgogne, New Belgium La Folie, Rodenbach Classic, Rodenbach Grand Cru, Vichtenaar Flemish Ale.

styles.name: Oud Bruin
text: Aroma: richly malty with fruity esters and aged sourness; medium to med-high esters (raisin, plum, fig, date, orange, black cherry, prune); med-low to med-high malt with caramel/toffee/treacle/chocolate; low spicy-pepper phenols optional; low sour aroma (should not become strongly acetic); no hops; aged ones can show nutty sherry-like oxidation.

Flavor: malty with fruity complexity, dark caramel/burnt sugar; medium to med-high fruit; slight sourness grows with age plus sherry notes giving "sweet-and-sour" profile; not strongly acetic; no hop flavor; restrained bitterness; malty balance; blending/sweetening alters finish.
Mouthfeel: medium to medium-full body; low to moderate carbonation; no astringency; stronger ones warm.

Key: dark reddish-brown to brown; long aging and blending of young/old beer; designed to be laid down; Pils malt, dark crystal, maize, small colour malt; low-alpha continental hops; Sacch + Lacto; carbonate/magnesium water; East Flanders (Liefmans); unrelated to Dutch dark lager of same name. Fruited to 29A.

Comparison: deeper malt (caramel, toffee, chocolate) and darker colour than Flanders Red; less acetic and maltier, fruit more malt-oriented, often higher ABV; unlike Lambic not spontaneous and no wheat.
Examples: Ichtegem Oud Bruin, Liefmans Goudenband, Liefmans Oud Bruin, Petrus Oud Bruin, pFriem Oud Bruin, Vanderghinste Bellegems Bruin.

styles.name: Lambic
text: Aroma: young ones sour and fruity; with age barnyard/earthy/goaty/hay/horse-blanket funk; fruit (light citrus, rind, pome, rhubarb) grows complex; malt light bready/grainy/honey/wheat if noticed; no enteric, smoky, cigar-like or cheesy faults; no hops.

Flavor: young = strong lactic sour with fruit; aged = more balanced/complex with funk; low bready/grainy malt; bitterness below threshold, sourness balances; no hop flavor; dry finish increasing with age; same faults as aroma.
Mouthfeel: light to med-light body, not watery; medium-high tart puckering without sharp astringency; traditionally virtually uncarbonated (bottled may pick up moderate).

Key: pale yellow to deep gold, hazy to good; single-batch UNBLENDED beer reflecting house character; usually served young (~6 months) from cask; pilsner malt + unmalted wheat; 3+ year old aged hops as preservative; SPONTANEOUS fermentation (wild yeast/bacteria) in neutral oak; vinegary/cidery = fault; with raw sugar = Faro; complex Brett takes 1+ year.
Comparison: simpler sourness, less complexity, more batch variation than Gueuze; uncarbonated draught vs Gueuze's bottled, very high carbonation.
Examples: Cantillon Grand Cru Bruocsella; draught lambic from Boon, De Cam, Cantillon, Drie Fonteinen, Lindemans, Timmermans, Girardin in Brussels cafes.

styles.name: Gueuze
text: Aroma: moderately sour with complex balanced funk (barnyard, leather, earthy, goaty, hay, horse blanket) plus light-mod fruit (citrus, rind, pome, rhubarb); supportive light bready/grainy/honey malt; light oak OK; no enteric/smoky/cigar/cheesy faults; no hops; complexity valued over intensity.

Flavor: sour and funky like aroma; low bready/grainy malt; bitterness low to none; no hop flavor; crisp dry finish, tart funky aftertaste; light oak/vanilla/honey OK; not one-dimensionally sour (moderately sour classic); may be aged.
Mouthfeel: light to med-light body, not watery; low-high tart puckering without sharp astringency; some very light warming; highly carbonated.

Key: golden, excellent clarity, thick rocky mousse head, effervescent; blend of 1-, 2-, 3-year lambics then cellared (refermentation in bottle); blenders often separate from brewers; "oude/vieille" most traditional; some modern producers sweeten (guidelines describe the dry traditional product); vinegary/cidery = fault.
Comparison: more complex and carbonated than Lambic; sourness not necessarily stronger but more developed wild character.
Examples: 3 Fonteinen Oud Gueuze, Cantillon Classic Gueuze, Girardin Gueuze 1882 (Black Label), Hanssens Oude Gueuze, Lindemans Gueuze Cuvee Rene, Oude Gueuze Boon.

styles.name: Fruit Lambic
text: Aroma: specified fruit dominates, blending with Gueuze-type aromatics plus fermented-fruit character.
Flavor: Gueuze profile plus noticeable fruit; traditional versions dry and tart; modern may be sweetened; fruit flavor fades with age (low to high intensity).
Mouthfeel: light to med-light body, not watery; low-high tart puckering; light warming possible; carbonation sparkling to nearly still.

Key: colour reflects fruit; fruit added to barrels (commonly midway through aging) so microbes ferment all fruit sugar; traditional fruit tart cherry (kriek), raspberry (framboise), modern peaches, apricots, grapes; fruit adds acidity and tannin; fermented fruit hard to identify; may be sweetened. Entry: must specify fruit, carbonation (low/med/high) and sweetness (low-none/med/high).
Comparison: a Gueuze with fruit, not just a sour fruit beer; wild character must be evident.
Examples: 3 Fonteinen Schaerbeekse Kriek, Cantillon Fou' Foune, Cantillon Lou Pepe Framboise, Cantillon Vigneronne, Hanssens Oude Kriek, Oude Kriek Boon.

styles.name: Gose
text: Aroma: light to moderate pome fruit; light slightly sharp sourness; noticeable lemony coriander up to moderate; light doughy bready/yeasty (uncooked sourdough); salt as faint sea-breeze freshness if noticed.

Flavor: noticeable sourness med-low to med-high; moderate bready/doughy malt; light-mod pome/stone fruit or lemon; light-mod salt up to threshold (noticeable, esp. initially, not overtly salty); very low bitterness; no hop flavor; dry fully attenuated finish; acidity balanced not forward; no THP.
Mouthfeel: high to very high carbonation; effervescent; med-light to medium-full body; salt gives tingly mouthwatering roundness; not heavy.

Key: unfiltered, moderate to full haze, yellow, tall tight white head; pilsner + wheat malt, restrained salt and coriander, Lacto (modern inoculated, more balanced than spontaneous historical versions); coriander should be fresh citrusy (not vegetal/celery/ham), salt clean sea/fresh salt (not metallic/iodine); Leipzig/Goslar history, revived 1980s; pronounced GOH-zeh; common base for fruited sours.
Comparison: less acidic than Berliner Weisse or Gueuze; coriander aroma like Witbier; haze like Weissbier.
Examples: Anderson Valley Gose, Bayerisch Bahnhof Leipziger Gose, Original Ritterguts Gose, Westbrook Gose.

styles.name: Witbier
text: Aroma: moderate bready malt (honey/vanilla notes); light grainy-spicy wheat; moderate perfumy-lemony coriander with herbal/spicy/peppery background; moderate zesty citrus-orange fruitiness; low spicy-herbal hop optional (typically absent); spices blend, not overdone.

Flavor: pleasant bready-grainy malt (honey/vanilla); moderate zesty orange-citrus; subtle balanced herbal-spicy (lemony coriander); hop flavor low to none (spicy-earthy), never overshadows spice; bitterness low to med-low; crisp dry finish, no bitter/harsh aftertaste.
Mouthfeel: med-light to medium, smooth, light creaminess; effervescent high carbonation; refreshing; no astringency; not thin or heavy.

Key: very pale straw to deep yellow, very cloudy milky shine from starch/yeast haze, dense white moussy head; unmalted wheat 30-60% (rest low-colour barley malt), maybe 5-10% raw oats/unmalted cereals; coriander seed + dried Curacao orange peel (sweet orange peel too); mild fruity-spicy Belgian ale yeast; no lactic sourness in modern versions; poor coriander can give ham/celery; perishable, fresh best; revived 1966 by Pierre Celis (Hoegaarden).
Comparison: low bitterness balance like Weissbier but spice and citrus come from additions more than yeast.
Examples: Allagash White, Blanche de Bruxelles, Celis White, Hoegaarden Wit, Ommegang Witte, St. Bernardus Witbier.

styles.name: Belgian Pale Ale
text: Aroma: moderate bready malt (toasty, biscuity, nutty; touch of light caramel/honey); moderate to mod-high fruit (pear, orange, apple, lemon, sometimes plum); low-mod spicy/herbal/floral hops; low peppery phenols optional; hops below malt and fruit.

Flavor: soft moderately malty start (toasty, biscuity, nutty, light caramel, honey); moderate to mod-high fruit; med-low to low hop character; med-high to med-low bitterness (helped by very low peppery phenols); dry to balanced finish; well balanced, no single high-intensity component.
Mouthfeel: medium to medium-light body; smooth; low alcohol warmth; medium to med-high carbonation.

Key: top-fermented, ALL-MALT (no adjuncts), not dry-hopped, no strong flavors; amber to copper, very good clarity; pale/character/caramel malts; English or continental hops; fruity low-phenol yeast; aka Speciale Belge; created after 1904 competition (De Koninck).
Comparison: fairly similar to English Strong Bitter (11C) but different yeast character and more varied malt; less yeast character than most Belgian beers.
Examples: De Koninck Bolleke, De Ryck Special, Palm, Palm Dobble.

styles.name: Biere de Garde
text: Aroma: prominent malty richness, often complex toasty-bready; low-mod esters; low spicy/peppery/herbal hops optional; generally clean (light spicy alcohol as it warms); paler versions less rich, a bit more hops.

Flavor: medium to high malty richness (toasty, biscuity, toffee, light caramel); low-mod esters and alcohol; medium-low bitterness, malty balance; medium-dry to dry finish, not sweet/cloying/heavy; low spicy-pepper-herbal hop optional; malt depth increases with colour, darker not roasted; paler can have slightly more hop flavor.
Mouthfeel: medium to med-light body, smooth creamy-silky; moderate to high carbonation; moderate alcohol warming, never hot.

Key: three colour versions (blonde, ambree amber, brune brown); entrant must specify colour; pale, Vienna, Munich base malts, crystal malts, sugar adjuncts possible; lager OR ale yeast fermented at cool ale temps then long cold conditioning (lagered); continental hops; "cellar/musty/moldy" character = mishandled import, not the style; oxidation adds caramel/fruit but harshness; Lille farmhouse tradition; Jenlain prototype amber (1940s).
Comparison: not a Saison (Saison is hoppy/bitter; BdG malty/smooth); malt profile closer to Bock.
Examples: Ch'Ti Blonde, Jenlain Ambree, La Choulette Brune, Russian River Perdition, Saint Sylvestre 3 Monts Blonde, Two Brothers Domaine DuPage.

styles.name: Belgian Blond Ale
text: Aroma: light-mod grainy-sweet, slightly toasty/crackery malt; subtle-moderate yeast with citrus esters (orange, lemon) and background spicy-peppery phenols; light earthy/spicy hops optional; light perfumy alcohol, honey/sugar-like sweetness; subtle but complex.

Flavor: light-mod grainy-sweet malt first; faint caramelized sugar/honey sweetness; medium bitterness, malt slightly ahead; moderate-low yeast profile (orange/lemon, slight pepper); light perfumy possible; light spicy/earthy hop; medium-dry to dry, smooth, soft finish with light alcohol and malt aftertaste.
Mouthfeel: medium-high to high carbonation (mouth-filling); medium body; light-mod smooth warmth; can be creamy.

Key: deep yellow to deep gold, very clear, dense creamy head, Belgian lace; most commercial examples 6.5-7%; almost lager-like clean; Belgian Pils malt, aromatic malts, sugar/adjuncts, Belgian abbey yeast, continental hops; spices not traditional (background only); post-WWII creation popularised by Leffe; abbey/artisanal "Blond" beers are not representative.
Comparison: similar strength/balance to Dubbel but gold without dark malt; like Golden Strong or Tripel but maltier, less bitter, lower alcohol.
Examples: Affligem Blond, Corsendonk Blond, Grimbergen Blond, La Trappe Blond, Leffe Blond, Val-Dieu Blond.

styles.name: Saison
text: Aroma: fruity-spicy yeast and hops; moderate-high esters (citrus, pome, stone fruit); low to mod-high spice often black pepper, not clove; hops low-mod continental (spicy, floral, earthy, fruity); malt overshadowed, lightly grainy; spices/herbs optional but not dominant; sourness optional; strong versions add alcohol and malt, table less intense, dark add dark-grain malt notes.

Flavor: balance of fruity-spicy yeast, hoppy bitterness and grainy malt; moderate to high bitterness; very dry finish; fruity/spicy med-low to med-high; hop flavor low-medium; malt low-medium soft grainy; very high attenuation, never sweet or heavy; bitter spicy aftertaste.
Mouthfeel: light to medium-low body; very high carbonation, effervescent; light warming optional (strong up to medium body and warming; table no warmth); sourness rare but optional.

Key: pale gold to deep amber (dark copper to brown possible), long-lasting rocky head, unfiltered/variable clarity; entrant must specify strength (table/standard/super) and colour (pale/dark), may name character grains; no correlation between strength and colour; must not be both sour AND bitter; Brett not typical (Brett saisons go to 28A); Grisette = Saison, Session Strength with wheat; pale base malt, cereal grains (wheat, oats, spelt, rye), sugary adjuncts, continental hops, spicy-fruity saison yeast; spices uncommon; Wallonian provision ale, Saison Dupont 1920s.
Comparison: pale standard version is a more attenuated, hoppier, more bitter Blond with stronger yeast character; super strength pale is like Tripel but more grainy/rustic and sometimes spicier.
Examples: Ellezelloise Saison 2000, Lefebvre Saison 1900, Saison Dupont, Saison de Pipaix, Saison Voisin, Boulevard Tank 7.

styles.name: Belgian Golden Strong Ale
text: Aroma: complex fruity esters, herbal hops, peppery alcohol over near-neutral malt; moderate-high esters (pome, esp. pear); herbal/floral/spicy hops low-mod; peppery/perfumy alcohol and phenols low-mod, soft not hot; malt slightly grainy-sweet at most.
Flavor: like aroma; pear-like esters, peppery alcohol, herbal hops, soft malt carry into long dry finish; medium to high bitterness accentuated by dryness and carbonation, lasting into aftertaste.
Mouthfeel: very highly carbonated, effervescent; light to medium body, lighter than gravity suggests; smooth but noticeable alcohol warmth, not hot/solventy.

Key: pale yellow to gold, good clarity, massive long-lasting rocky head with Belgian lace; Pilsner malt with substantial sugar adjuncts; continental hops; fruity Belgian yeast; soft water; spicing not traditional; devil names (Duvel) reference potency; traditionally bottle-conditioned; Moortgat, post-WWI.
Comparison: often confused with Tripel but usually paler, lighter-bodied, crisper, drier; yeast favors esters (pome) over spice, more late hop.
Examples: Brigand, Delirium Tremens, Duvel, Judas, Lucifer, Russian River Damnation.

styles.name: Belgian Single
text: Aroma: med-low to med-high Belgian yeast fruity-spicy; med-low to medium spicy/floral hops (rarely light herbal/citrus spice); low to med-low bready/crackery/grainy/honey malt; varied fruit (apple, pear, grapefruit, lemon, orange, peach, apricot); phenols black pepper or clove; bubblegum inappropriate.

Flavor: light honeyed-biscuit/bready/cracker malt; grainy but soft palate; crisp dry hoppy-bitter finish; moderate spicy/floral hop flavor; moderate esters; light-mod phenols; medium to high bitterness accentuated by dryness; yeast and hop character linger.
Mouthfeel: med-light to medium body; smooth; med-high to high carbonation (can be prickly); no noticeable alcohol warmth.

Key: pale yellow to medium gold, good clarity, billowy white head with lacing; Pilsner malt, Belgian yeast, continental hops; attenuation generally 85%+; monk's table beer (aka Brother's beer/"Blond" - term avoided to prevent confusion with Belgian Blond); often not available outside monastery; formerly "Trappist Single".

Comparison: a Belgian top-fermented take on German Pils (pale, hoppy, attenuated, strong Belgian yeast); less sweet, more attenuated, less character malt, more hop-centered than Belgian Pale Ale; like a much smaller, more hopped Tripel rather than a smaller Blond.
Examples: Chimay Gold, La Trappe Puur, Russian River Redemption, St. Bernardus Extra 4, Westmalle Extra, Westvleteren Blond.

styles.name: Belgian Dubbel
text: Aroma: moderate to mod-strong rich malt with hints of chocolate, caramelized sugar, toast (never roasted/burnt); moderate esters, dark/dried fruit (raisin, plum), sometimes pome or banana; low-mod spicy-peppery phenols; hops typically absent (low spicy/herbal/floral possible); malt strongest in balance; low soft perfumy alcohol optional.

Flavor: like aroma; medium-low to medium bitterness but malt always most prominent; esters/phenols add complexity, alcohol not typically tasted; malty-rich, sometimes sweet, finishes moderately dry with malty aftertaste.
Mouthfeel: smooth, medium to medium-full body; medium-high carbonation; low warmth optional, never hot/solventy.

Key: dark amber to copper with reddish depth, generally clear, large dense long-lasting creamy off-white head; most commercial examples 6.5-7%; spicy-estery Belgian yeast; impression of complex grist though traditional versions simple, with caramelized sugar syrup/unrefined sugars doing much of the work; continental hops; spices not typical; can taste sweet but actually fairly dry; Westmalle 1922.
Comparison: perhaps like Dunkles Bock but with Belgian yeast and sugar character; similar strength/balance to Belgian Blond but richer malt and esters; less strong/intense than Dark Strong.
Examples: Chimay Red, Corsendonk Bruin, La Trappe Dubbel, Rochefort 6, St. Bernardus Pater 6, Westmalle Dubbel.

styles.name: Belgian Tripel
text: Aroma: complex seamless bouquet; moderate to significant spiciness (peppery, sometimes clove-like phenols), moderate fruity esters (citrus: orange/lemon; slight ripe banana possible), low soft spicy alcohol, low hops (spicy, floral, perfumy optional), light soft grainy-sweet/honey-like malt.

Flavor: like aroma; esters low-mod, phenols low-mod, hops low-mod, alcohol low, all well combined; medium to high bitterness accentuated by dry finish; moderate bitterness in aftertaste with substantial spicy-fruity yeast; should not be sweet.
Mouthfeel: med-light to medium body, lighter than gravity suggests; highly carbonated, effervescent; little to no warming (deceptive alcohol); not heavy.

Key: deep yellow to pale amber, good clarity, long-lasting creamy rocky head with lace; Pilsner malt, often pale sugar adjuncts; continental hops; spicy-fruity Belgian yeast; spices not traditional (background only); soft water; "sneaky" strong; most traditional versions >=30 IBU and very dry; Westmalle 1931.
Comparison: may resemble Golden Strong but slightly darker, fuller-bodied, more phenols less esters, fewer late hops; should not seem like a blond Barleywine.
Examples: Chimay Tripel, La Rulles Tripel, La Trappe Tripel, St. Bernardus Tripel, Val-Dieu Triple, Westmalle Tripel.

styles.name: Belgian Dark Strong Ale
text: Aroma: complex fairly intense rich malt and deep fruit, accentuated by spicy phenols and alcohol; malt mod-high to high, deep bready-toasty base with dark caramel, no dark/roasted-malt impression; esters strong to mod-low (raisin, plum, dried cherry, fig, date, prune); low-mod black pepper or vanilla phenols (not clove); soft spicy/perfumy/rose-like alcohol low-mod, never hot/solventy; hops usually not noticeable.

Flavor: rich complex malt but not heavy in finish; same malt/ester/phenol/alcohol/hop notes as aroma; sweet impression if bitterness low; usually moderately dry to dry finish (may be up to moderately sweet); medium-low to moderate bitterness, alcohol helps balance; flavors blend smoothly, often improve with age; not syrupy.
Mouthfeel: high carbonation but not sharp; smooth noticeable warmth; body medium-light to medium-full and creamy (most medium).

Key: deep amber to deep coppery-brown ("dark" = deeper than gold, not black), huge dense moussy cream/light-tan head, usually clear; aka Belgian Quad (mainly outside Belgium; "Quadruple" is a specific beer); wider interpretation range (traditional drier, modern commercial can be sweet and full); "Grand Cru" is a quality claim not a style; spicy-estery Belgian yeast; complex-seeming grist but traditionally simple with caramelized sugar syrup/unrefined sugars; continental hops; spices not typical; Westvleteren pre-WWII.
Comparison: like a larger Dubbel, fuller body and more malt richness; not as bitter/hoppy as Tripel but similar strength.
Examples: Achel Extra Bruin, Boulevard The Sixth Glass, Chimay Blue, Rochefort 10, St. Bernardus Abt 12, Westvleteren 12.
